title: The swap that goes in circles
hook: Max likes every swap he makes, and he pays for each one. Where does that leave him?

knows: preferring one thing to another; paying a little for something you prefer
doesNotKnow: that preferences in a circle let someone sell you swaps for ever, which is why choice models assume preferences are transitive

misconception: Preferences that go in a circle are odd but harmless.
objective: The learner can explain that with circular preferences every swap is wanted yet 3 swaps return the same fruit, so 6 swaps cost 60¢ for nothing, while ranked (transitive) preferences stop the swaps at the favourite; and that this is why choice models assume transitivity.

claims.text: With apple over banana, banana over cherry and cherry over apple, starting from a cherry, the preferred swaps go cherry, banana, apple, cherry: 3 swaps bring the cherry back for 30¢, and 6 swaps cost 60¢ and end on the cherry.
claims.source: replay('circle', n) in src/demos/math/the-swap-that-goes-in-circles/Demo.tsx: each fruit has exactly one fruit Max prefers to it (the next round the circle), so every offer round the circle is taken. Builder's node re-run (scratch j16check.mjs, same rules): circle 6 cherry>banana>apple>cherry>banana>apple>cherry, 60; circle 3 ... >cherry, 30. Brief check J16 (node company/courses/ncm/checks/rejudged-four.mjs): six cherry 60, three cherry 30. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: With apple over banana over cherry, and offers coming one fruit at a time round the circle (banana for the cherry, apple for the banana, then cherry for the apple), the swaps stop at the apple after 2 (20¢): he refuses the cherry.

Builder's node re-run: ranked 6 cherry>banana>apple, 2 swaps, 20. J16 ranked apple 20 2. The offer order is the lesson's (the stage's arrows); with a direct cherry-for-apple offer he would stop at the apple after 1. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: A group's majority can still go round in a circle even when every voter's preferences are ranked: three voters ranking A > B > C, B > C > A and C > A > B give A beating B, B beating C and C beating A, each 2 to 1.

claims.text: Ranked (transitive) preferences mean that if Max prefers apple to banana and banana to cherry, he prefers apple to cherry, so there is no circle to sell him ('if Max prefers apple to banana and banana to cherry, he prefers apple to cherry, so there is no circle to sell him').
claims.source: Definition of transitivity (Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 23, section 23.2 unconfirmed: if X is preferred to Y and Y to Z, then X is preferred to Z), applied to the lesson's ranked mode. 'No circle to sell him' is what the stage shows: in ranked mode (replay('ranked', 6) in Demo.tsx) the apple -> cherry offer is refused (dashed, 'refused'), so the swaps stop at the apple after 2. Builder-written (W-1570 fix round, 2026-10-16); unverified.

recall.question: Sam prefers tea to coffee, coffee to juice and juice to tea, and pays 5p to swap for a drink he prefers. Why can a shopkeeper profit from Sam for ever?
options: His preferences go in a circle, so every swap he wants leads back to where he started
He always pays more than each drink is worth
He cannot tell the drinks apart
recall.why: With circular preferences each swap is wanted, but three swaps bring the same drink back, so he pays again and again for nothing. Ranked (transitive) preferences would stop at his favourite.
